title: One family (Genesis Rabbah 24:7)
hookLine: Akiva names love your neighbor as the great principle; Ben Azzai names the book of Adam's generations, one human family
tomorrow: why would Noah plant trees he meant to cut down?

lines: ONE RULE THAT SUMS IT UP?
BEN AZZAI: A LIST OF NAMES.
cards: Ask a group of friends for the one rule that sums it all up, and you'll get as many answers as friends. Two sages had that argument about the whole Torah.
Rabbi Akiva named a line from Leviticus: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Ben Azzai named a different line, one that's easy to skim past, from a list of names in Genesis.

teach.b: His verse: "This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made He him." A family tree. Ben Azzai calls it a greater principle.
Why pick a list of names over love?
Because love your neighbor leaves a door open: who counts as my neighbor? The family tree shuts it. Every person you meet comes out of that one book, made in the likeness of God.
Genesis Rabbah adds Rabbi Tanhuma's sharp line: don't say, since I was put down, let my fellow be put down too.
If you do, know whom you're putting down: one made in God's likeness. So, who is my family? In Ben Azzai's answer, everyone in the book of Adam.
A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.
Christians read in the book of Acts that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth."
The same picture: one family, from one start. And one honest difference. Ben Azzai argues from a Torah genealogy and God's likeness.
In Acts, Paul says it in a speech in Athens that ends by pointing to Jesus, raised from the dead. Two traditions, each speaking from its own book, standing close on this one.

how: Ben Azzai's and Rabbi Akiva's sayings are often studied side by side in Jewish classes on how to treat others; the verse from Leviticus is also read in the synagogue in its yearly turn.

o: the people who share your home and your blood
a people bound together by one shared faith
everyone in one family tree, from the book of Adam

games.q: who said which — tap the pairs.
p: the book of the generations of Adam

s: all religions teach exactly the same thing about humanity
Ben Azzai and Acts stand close on one family, but each says it from its own book, and differently.
Ben Azzai called a list of names a greater principle
the book of the generations of Adam: one human family.
Ben Azzai's family tree means only the Jewish people
it's the book of Adam: everyone, each made in God's likeness.

games.q: at dinner your kid asks: is the new boy in class, from another country, part of our family? what can you say from this lesson?
o: yes: in the book of Adam we're one family, all made in God's likeness.
no; family means the people who share our religion and our home.
only after he's lived here a while and learned how we do things.
games.why: Ben Azzai's verse is the whole human family tree. and Rabbi Tanhuma adds: whoever you put down is made in God's likeness.

practice: Close your eyes and bring back one face from today that you don't know: a cashier, a driver, someone in line. Hold that face for a few breaths and say inside, from the book of Adam.
Then let a second face come, and a third, and let the family grow until the bell.

wordCard.voice: One family: Ben Azzai's great principle, the book of the generations of Adam. Everyone in one family tree, each made in God's likeness.

orig.note: Hebrew: the generations of Adam (Genesis 5:1), Ben Azzai's great principle.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: one family, the stranger in line included, all from the same book. See you tomorrow.
